section.title: Justice, Discipline, and Pride
section.sectionRationale: Closing the Hezekiah collection, 25:1 to 29:27, this chapter presses the fate of the stiff-necked, the effect of righteous versus wicked rule on a groaning or rejoicing people, the discipline of children and servants, and the true safety of trusting the LORD rather than fearing man.
section.thesis: A people flourishes under righteous rule and groans under the wicked, so wisdom means welcoming correction while there is still time, disciplining children toward rest and delight, and trusting the LORD rather than the fear of man, which is always a snare.
section.frameNote: Four clusters: the stiff-necked and sudden ruin, righteous rule and its effect on a people; discipline and the rod that gives rest; anger, flattery, and the poor man's common light with the oppressor; the fear of man as a snare, and safety in trusting the LORD.

units.label: The stiff-necked and righteous rule
units.note: when the righteous flourish, the people rejoice

verses.text: A man who remains stiff-necked after much reproof will suddenly be shattered beyond recovery.
When the righteous flourish, the people rejoice, but when the wicked rule, the people groan.
A man who loves wisdom brings joy to his father, but a companion of prostitutes squanders his wealth.
By justice a king brings stability to the land, but a man who exacts tribute demolishes it.
A man who flatters his neighbor spreads a net for his feet.
An evil man is caught by his own sin, but a righteous one sings and rejoices.
The righteous consider the cause of the poor, but the wicked have no regard for such concerns.

units.label: Discipline and the rod that gives rest

verses.text: Mockers inflame a city, but the wise turn away anger.
If a wise man goes to court with a fool, there will be raving and laughing with no resolution.
Men of bloodshed hate a blameless man, but the upright care for his life.
A fool vents all his anger, but a wise man holds it back.
If a ruler listens to lies, all his officials will be wicked.
The poor man and the oppressor have this in common: The LORD gives light to the eyes of both.
A king who judges the poor with fairness, his throne will be established forever.
A rod of correction imparts wisdom, but a child left to himself disgraces his mother.
When the wicked thrive, rebellion increases; but the righteous will see their downfall.
Discipline your son, and he will give you rest; he will bring delight to your soul.

units.label: Vision, correction, and the poor man's common light
units.note: where there is no vision, the people cast off restraint

verses.text: Where there is no {{chazon|vision}}, the people cast off restraint; but blessed is he who keeps the Law.
A servant cannot be corrected by words alone; though he understands, he will not respond.
Do you see a man who speaks in haste? There is more hope for a fool than for him.
A servant pampered from his youth will bring grief in the end.
An angry man stirs up dissension, and a hot-tempered man abounds in transgression.
A man's pride will bring him low, but a humble spirit will obtain honor.
A partner to a thief hates his own soul; he receives the oath, but does not testify.

units.label: The fear of man is a snare
units.note: trust in the LORD is set securely on high

verses.text: The {{yirah|fear}} of man is a snare, but whoever trusts in the LORD is set securely on high.
Many seek the ruler's favor, but a man receives justice from the LORD.
An unjust man is detestable to the righteous, and one whose way is upright is detestable to the wicked.

chazon.gloss: Vision, prophetic revelation. Verse 18 says where this is absent, people cast off restraint, connecting a community's moral order directly to whether it receives and heeds God's revealed word, not merely to strong leadership or good ideas in general.

yirah.gloss: Fear, dread. Verse 25 says this fear of man, not the fear of the LORD, is a snare, a deliberate contrast within the book's vocabulary: fearing God rightly leads to life, 14:27, while fearing people wrongly entangles and enslaves.

basic.context: This chapter closes the Hezekiah collection by pressing hard on the difference righteous versus wicked leadership makes for a whole community, the discipline needed to raise children and correct servants, and the snare of fearing what people think instead of trusting the LORD. It moves from public life to the household to the individual heart, showing wisdom's reach across every level of life.
basic.hermeneutics: These proverbs describe patterns of moral and social cause and effect under God's ordered world; they train discernment about leadership, discipline, and fear rather than promising an identical outcome in every single case. Verse 18's famous line about vision has often been detached from its context about keeping God's law and applied to generic goal-setting, a reading the Hebrew itself does not support.
basic.originalLanguages: Chazon, vision, verse 18, refers to prophetic revelation from God, not human ambition or planning, so that a community without it 'casts off restraint,' becoming lawless precisely because it has no word from God to order its life; the second half of the verse, 'blessed is he who keeps the Law,' confirms this reading. Yirah, fear, verse 25, is used here of a wrongly placed dread of people, deliberately set against the rightly placed fear of the LORD that runs through the whole book.
basic.typology: Verse 18's absence of vision leading to lawlessness anticipates the New Testament's emphasis on the necessity of the revealed word of Christ for ordering the church's life, since faith itself comes by hearing that word, Romans 10:17. Verse 25's contrast between the fear of man and trust in the LORD foreshadows the boldness believers gain through union with Christ, who frees them from the fear of both man and death, Hebrews 2:14-15.
basic.christ: Verse 25's warning that the fear of man is a snare while trust in the LORD brings safety anticipates the freedom Christ secures for His people, who through His death has delivered all who through fear of death were subject to lifelong slavery, Hebrews 2:14-15, breaking every human power's grip over the believer's conscience. And verse 18's insistence that a people perish without vision, that is, without God's revealed word, points toward Christ, the Word made flesh, John 1:14, apart from whom no true and lasting restraint or order can be found.
basic.god: God gives light to the eyes of poor and oppressor alike, verse 13, showing His common grace toward all people even while His justice ultimately distinguishes between them. He is the true source of justice a ruler's favor cannot supply, verse 26, and the sure refuge for anyone who trusts Him rather than fearing what people can do, verse 25.
basic.crossReferences: Hebrews 2:14-15 fulfills the freedom from the fear of man promised in verse 25. John 1:14 echoes the necessity of God's revealed word behind the vision of verse 18. Romans 10:17 echoes the priority of hearing God's word for ordered, faithful life. Hebrews 12:11 develops the discipline that yields rest, echoing verse 17.
basic.oneStory: Proverbs 29 shows that a community flourishes under righteous rule, that children and servants need real discipline to find rest, and that fearing people is a snare while trusting the LORD is safety. This whole vision reaches its fulfillment in Christ, the Word who orders life rightly and who frees His people from every fear but the fear of God.

context.literary:
Proverbs 29 is the last chapter of the collection that opens at 25:1, and it is arranged to end it with a bang. The opening verse and the closing verse both deal with a fixed attitude: the neck that will not bend after much reproof, verse 1, and the mutual detestation of the unjust and the upright, verse 27. The first is a person who is shattered; the last is a world divided in two. Between them the chapter keeps returning to a handful of contrasts: righteous against wicked, wise against fool, and the one who listens against the one who will not.

Three clusters are easy to see. Verses 2 to 16 are chiefly about rulers and the public square. Verse 2 sets rejoicing against groaning, verse 4 sets justice against exactions, verse 12 warns that a ruler who listens to lies finds his officials turning wicked, and verse 14 offers the long throne of the king who judges the poor with fairness. Verses 15 to 21 turn to the household, with the rod, the son, the servant and the child. Verses 22 to 27 move inward to the heart and its anger, pride, loyalties and fears.

Two sayings in the middle act as hinges. Verse 13, in which the poor man and the oppressor have one thing in common, sits at the junction of the public and private sections and reminds the reader that rulers and ruled stand under the same Giver. Verse 18 interrupts the run of household sayings with a line about revelation and law, as if to say that everything on either side of it depends on a word from God. The last verses, 25 and 26, then turn the whole to a decision: where will you put your trust?
context.historical:
This chapter looks like it was written from within a royal court, since so much of it concerns what a king should and should not do. The men of Hezekiah, who copied these sayings, served a king whose reign included the fall of the northern kingdom and the Assyrian invasion of Judah. Verse 12, about a ruler who listens to lies and finds that his officials become wicked, would have rung true to anyone who had seen a court ruled by flatterers.

The household described in verses 15 to 21 is a large and working one. A child, a son, a servant and a pampered servant all live under one roof, and the father is responsible for all of them. Servants in Israel were part of the family, and correction of them was a domestic matter. The rod was a shepherd's staff and a teacher's tool. The household was also the place where the Torah was taught: parents were told to speak of God's commands when sitting at home and when walking along the road, Deuteronomy 6:6 and 7.

Verse 24 describes a legal situation. A person who partners with a thief hears the public curse or oath summoning witnesses and yet says nothing. The Torah laid a guilt on anyone who heard such a charge about something he had witnessed and did not testify, Leviticus 5:1. The village court sat at the gate, and justice there depended on witnesses prepared to speak.

Verse 25 should be read against the Assyrian crisis. When the Rabshakeh stood outside Jerusalem, he pressed Hezekiah's people with a question about the basis of their confidence, 2 Kings 18:19, and the text commends Hezekiah because he trusted in the LORD, 2 Kings 18:5. The fear of a great king was a snare that faced them in the flesh.
context.canonical:
The chapter's final saying about fear and trust is one of the most repeated themes in Scripture. The psalmist asks what man can do to him, Psalm 118:6, and Hebrews 13:6 takes up the same confession for the church. Jesus tells His followers not to fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul, Matthew 10:28. Peter and the apostles answer the council with 'We must obey God rather than men,' Acts 5:29. John records the opposite choice: leaders who believed in Jesus but would not confess Him for fear of the Pharisees, because they loved praise from men more than praise from God, John 12:42 and 43.

Verse 18 stands near the heart of the canon's concern for the word of God. Amos 8:11 and 12 imagines a famine of hearing the words of the LORD. First Samuel 3:1 describes the dark days when the word of the LORD was rare and visions were scarce. At the other end of the story, the Son is the Word who became flesh, John 1:14, and Hebrews 1:1 and 2 says God has spoken finally by His Son.

The sayings about discipline lead to Hebrews 12:5 to 11, which quotes Proverbs 3:11 and 12 and reads the Father's training of His children in the light of Proverbs. Ephesians 6:4 adds the gentle counterweight for fathers, not to provoke children to wrath.

Verse 13 echoes Proverbs 22:2, that the rich and the poor have the LORD as maker, and Jesus' teaching that God sends sun and rain on the evil and the good, Matthew 5:45. Verse 14 echoes the promise to David that his throne would be established forever, 2 Samuel 7:16, and on the prayer of Psalm 72 that the king would deliver the needy.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
The editors close the Hezekiah collection by pressing the sort of question a king, a father and an ordinary man must face. A king is asked whether he will govern by justice or by extraction, and whether he will let lies into his court. A father is asked whether he will love his son enough to correct him, and a master whether he will correct a servant who will not hear words alone. Everyone is asked whom he fears.

The first hearers were meant to notice how much is at stake in the unseen. The fool who vents all his anger, verse 11, and the man who speaks in haste, verse 20, cause damage that cannot be called back. A city is inflamed by mockers, verse 8, and a household is soured by quarrels, verse 22. The wise person is the one who turns anger away, who holds back his spirit, and who treats the poor man's case as his own business, verse 7.

The chapter also wants hearers to see that revelation and restraint belong together. Verse 18 is placed at the centre of the household sayings because a home without the word of God is a home with nothing to order discipline. The teacher is not pleading for harshness but for a loving training that has a purpose: rest and delight for the parent, wisdom for the child, verses 15 and 17.

At the end, the hearer is given a choice about fear. The people around us, rulers included, are never the final judges. The teacher wants his hearers to leave unafraid of what people can do and afraid only of failing the LORD.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
Most of the chapter is description and wisdom for judging well, but some lines are close to commands. Verse 17, discipline your son, and verse 7's picture of those who consider the cause of the poor are exhortations. Others, such as verse 2 on rejoicing and groaning, report what is observed and ask the reader to draw the lesson.

Two of the best known lines need care. Verse 15 speaks of the rod of correction and verse 17 says to discipline your son. These belong to a book that also says that the LORD disciplines the one He loves as a father the son in whom he delights, Proverbs 3:11 and 12. The purpose is wisdom, rest and delight, not harm. The text assumes a loving household in which correction is a part of training, not a licence for cruelty, and Paul adds that fathers should not provoke their children to anger, Ephesians 6:4. How correction is carried out today is a matter for wisdom and the law of the land, and this chapter does not lay down a method.

Verse 18 is often taken as a slogan for business and church leadership, but in context it concerns revelation and the law, and applying it to goals and strategy borrows its authority from a different subject. Verse 25 is a promise that carries forward, but it is not a guarantee that no human being will ever harm the one who trusts. It is the claim that the believer's ultimate security is not in the hands of people.

debates.question: Does verse 18, 'where there is no vision, the people cast off restraint,' apply broadly to any lack of inspiring goals or leadership, or specifically to the absence of God's revealed word?

views.label: It applies broadly to any absence of vision, purpose, or inspiring leadership
views.case: The verse is frequently quoted in leadership and organizational contexts to mean that any group without a compelling vision or goal will drift into disorder.

views.label: It refers specifically to prophetic revelation from God, confirmed by its own second half
views.case: Chazon in the Old Testament consistently denotes prophetic revelation, and the verse's own parallel clause, 'blessed is he who keeps the Law,' anchors the vision in God's revealed word rather than generic human vision-casting; the concern is a famine of God's word, as in Amos 8:11-12, not merely uninspired leadership.

debates.bearing: Reading the verse in its specific, canonical sense, the absence of God's own revelation and law, rather than generic organizational vision, keeps the proverb's warning aimed where the text itself points: a people perishes not for lack of ambition but for lack of God's word to order its life.

debates.question: Does the rod of verses 15 and 17 require physical punishment of children?

views.label: Yes, it commends literal corporal discipline
views.case: The rod is a physical object, and Proverbs 13:24 and 23:13 and 14 speak of striking a child with it and sparing it as a sign of not loving him. Many Christians have taken these texts to authorise measured physical correction as part of loving parenting.

views.label: The rod is a figure for firm, loving correction in general
views.case: The word for rod also names a shepherd's staff and a ruler's sceptre, so the image may stand for authority exercised for the child's good, as in Psalm 23:4, and not specifically for blows. Proverbs elsewhere makes correction a matter of words, reproof and training, and Hebrews 12 reads the Father's discipline as training, not only pain.

views.label: It reflects an ancient setting whose method we need not repeat
views.case: The proverbs reflect the discipline of their time, as the law of Moses regulated slavery and divorce without endorsing them as ideals. What carries forward is the commitment to correct for the child's good, while modern knowledge and law shape how that is done.

debates.bearing: All three views agree that to leave a child to himself is a failure of love, verse 15, and that correction is for the child's wisdom and the home's rest. They differ over the method, so parents should weigh the text prayerfully, avoid any discipline done in anger, and never let a proverb become an excuse for abuse.

study.originalLanguages:
The chapter's best known saying is verse 18, and its key word is chazon, from the verb to see. The word names what a prophet sees, a revelation from God, and the matching clause, blessed is he who keeps the Law (torah), says what the revelation is for. First Samuel 3:1 uses the same noun for the visions that were scarce in Eli's day, and Amos 8:11 and 12 pictures a famine of hearing the word of the LORD. The phrase translated cast off restraint is a single verb, para, which means to let loose or let go. It is the same verb Exodus 32:25 uses when Moses saw that the people were out of control because Aaron had let them run wild. The golden calf is the scene behind the proverb: a people without the mediator of the word, left to itself, goes wild.

In verse 25 the word that the BSB translates as fear is, in the Hebrew, a different word from the usual fear of the LORD. It is a noun for trembling, the same family as the verb used of Isaac when he began to tremble violently, Genesis 27:33, and of the panic that spread among the Philistines, 1 Samuel 14:15. The proverb names a trembling before people, and the snare is the thing that trap catches: a snare in the Old Testament is also the thing that false gods will be to Israel, Exodus 23:33. The trembling itself becomes the trap, because a person who dreads others can be steered by them. The one who trusts, again from the verb batach, is set securely on high, a verb that Proverbs 18:10 uses of the righteous who run to the name of the LORD and are safe.

Verse 1 describes a man who stiffens his neck, an image from the ox that refuses the yoke, and the phrase is the one used of Israel as a stiff-necked people in Exodus 32:9. His end is described as sudden and beyond recovery, with the same words Proverbs 6:15 uses and that 2 Chronicles 36:16 applies to Judah, wrath that rose until there was no remedy.

Verse 4 names the destructive king as a man of terumah. That is the ordinary word for a contribution lifted up and set apart for the sanctuary, as in Exodus 25:2. The BSB footnote offers heavy taxing or bribes. The word here has been turned: a gift meant for God becomes a levy squeezed from the people.

Verse 15 speaks of a child left to himself, using the verb to send away, to let go. The child is the one who has been released without restraint, a mirror of the people in verse 18 who have been let loose.

Verse 13 calls the oppressor a man of oppressions and says that the LORD gives light to the eyes of both. The light of the eyes is the gift of life itself in the Old Testament, as in Psalm 13:3, and so both men owe it to Him.

typology.type: The king who judges the poor with fairness, Proverbs 29:14
typology.fulfillment: The verse promises an established throne to the king who judges the poor with fairness. God's promise to David was that his throne would be established forever, 2 Samuel 7:16, and Psalm 72 prays that such a king would deliver the needy who cry out and have no helper. Jesus is the fulfilment: He is the Son who will reign forever, Luke 1:32 and 33, and the king who identifies with the hungry, the stranger and the prisoner, Matthew 25:35 and 36. The earthly kings fell short, since Hezekiah himself had failures. Christ alone judges the poor with perfect fairness.

The rod gives wisdom, and the Bible sees in it a picture of the Father's training. Hebrews 12:5 to 11 reads God's discipline of His children through Proverbs 3:11 and 12 and says it yields a harvest of righteousness and peace. The Son Himself learned obedience from what He suffered, Hebrews 5:8, and He is the Shepherd whose rod and staff comfort, Psalm 23:4. The correspondence is real but limited, because human parents correct imperfectly, and God's discipline of believers never carries the penalty of sin, which Christ has borne.

typology.type: The fear of man and the Son who was not afraid, Proverbs 29:25
typology.fulfillment: The proverb contrasts being caught in a snare with being set on high. Jesus was surrounded by people who could harm Him and yet was not controlled by them. He set His face to go to Jerusalem, Luke 9:51, and went forward to meet those who came for Him, John 18:4. When His disciples fled out of fear, Matthew 26:56, He remained. The type is exceeded because Christ's courage was not temperament but trust, 1 Peter 2:23, and by it He frees His people from fear, Hebrews 2:14 and 15.

typology.type: Where there is no vision, Proverbs 29:18
typology.fulfillment: The proverb says a people without revelation runs wild, and the history of Israel after the golden calf proves it. Amos 8:11 imagines a famine of hearing the word of the LORD. The answer is the arrival of the Word Himself. John 1:14 says the Word became flesh and dwelt among us, and Hebrews 1:1 and 2 says that in these last days God has spoken by His Son. The pattern is real, though the word in Proverbs is the law and the prophets, and it would be wrong to say the proverb itself speaks of Jesus.

study.christ:
The chapter leads to Christ by three roads: the king, the word and the one who is not afraid.

Take the king first. Verses 2, 4, 12, 14 and 16 are a catalogue of what happens under a good and a bad ruler, and verse 14 sets out the pattern of a good one: he judges the poor with fairness, and his throne is established forever. That phrase was heard against the promise to David, 2 Samuel 7:16, and Israel waited for a son of David who would do it. The Gospels present Jesus as the son who has come. The angel tells Mary that the Lord God will give Him the throne of His father David and that His kingdom will never end, Luke 1:32 and 33. The same king gives sight to the blind, preaches good news to the poor, Luke 4:18, and is not partial: He receives Zacchaeus, who had defrauded others, Luke 19:8 to 10, and He calls the poor in spirit blessed, Matthew 5:3. Verse 13 observes that the LORD gives light to the eyes of both, and in Christ that light is also moral, for He is the true Light who gives light to everyone, John 1:9.

Now the word. Verse 18 concerns a people without revelation who run wild. The New Testament says that revelation has taken a human face. 'The Word became flesh and made His dwelling among us,' John 1:14. He is the vision that the people were missing, and Hebrews 1:1 and 2 says that God has spoken to us by His Son. The rest of the verse, blessed is he who keeps the Law, is taken up by Jesus when He says that those who hear the word of God and keep it are blessed, Luke 11:28. It would be wrong to say that Proverbs 29:18 predicts Christ. It is better to say that it describes the famine He ends.

Finally, the one who is not afraid. Verse 25 sets the fear of man against trust in the LORD, and Jesus lives that trust. He stood before Pilate and answered, John 18:36 to 37. When the crowd came with swords and clubs He went out to meet them, John 18:4. And on the cross, He entrusted Himself to Him who judges justly, 1 Peter 2:23. He did not escape the snare, but He was never caught in it, and His resurrection is the sign that those who trust the LORD are set securely on high, as the proverb promises. Those united to Him share that security, for He has freed those who were held in slavery all their lives by their fear of death, Hebrews 2:15.

A guardrail applies here. The sayings about the rod, the servant and the court are practical, and they do not need to be turned into Christ-code. They point to Him by raising the need for a perfect ruler, a revealed word and a fearless trust.
study.god:
Verse 13 gives the chapter's foundation for its doctrine of God: the poor man and the oppressor have this in common, the LORD gives light to the eyes of both. This is the language of common grace. The same God who will judge the oppressor keeps him alive, lets him see, and gives him time. It is the proverb that stands behind Jesus' teaching that the Father makes His sun rise on the evil and the good, Matthew 5:45.

God is also the one to whom justice finally belongs. Verse 26 says many seek the ruler's favour but justice comes from the LORD. It does not mean that earthly courts are worthless, since the same chapter praises the king who judges with fairness. It means that human rulers are subordinate: they are the instruments of the one who is the true Judge. The chapter even gives a hint of how that justice works: the wicked will rule for a time, but the righteous will see their downfall, verse 16.

He is the God who speaks. The blessing in verse 18 is for those who keep the law, and the curse is a loss of the word. This is a God who has chosen to be known through a spoken revelation and who treats the withdrawal of that word as a severe judgment, as Amos 8:11 describes. A people who have it have the greatest gift, and a people who lack it are unrestrained.

He is a God of secure refuge. The verb for set securely on high is used elsewhere of the strong tower of His name, Proverbs 18:10. Verse 25 implies that He is more reliable than any ruler and has a power that no human can finally remove.

And He is a Father who disciplines. The rod, the reproof and the training of the chapter reflect, in a small way, what Proverbs 3:11 and 12 and Hebrews 12:6 say of Him: He disciplines the one He loves. The chapter holds together His patience, in the much reproof of verse 1, with the sudden end that awaits the person who never bends.

For worship, the chapter calls us to receive correction as a gift from the Father, to listen to His word as the life of the community, and to bring our fear of other people to the One in whose hands they are.

crossReferences.note: Moses sees that the people are out of control because Aaron had let them run wild. The verb is the one behind 'cast off restraint' in verse 18, and the golden calf is the clearest picture of a people left without the word.

In the days of Eli the word of the LORD was rare and visions were scarce. It gives the word 'vision' of verse 18 its Old Testament use as revelation from God, and shows what a famine of the word looked like.

A famine, not of bread or water, but of hearing the words of the LORD. Verse 18 states the same loss from the angle of its effects, a people who cast off restraint, while Amos shows the divine judgment behind it.

Anyone who hears a public charge about something he has witnessed and fails to testify bears the iniquity. This is the legal backdrop of verse 24, where the partner of a thief hears the oath and says nothing, and so harms his own soul.

The rich and the poor have this in common: the LORD is Maker of them all. It is a sister to verse 13, which says that both the poor man and the oppressor receive light for the eyes from the LORD, and it shows the shared source of human dignity.

The promise that David's house and kingdom would endure forever and his throne be established forever. Verse 14 borrows this vocabulary for the king who judges the poor with fairness, and ties the long throne to justice.

The prayer for the king that he would deliver the needy who cry out, pity the poor and redeem them from oppression. It is the fullest expression of verse 14 and 7, and describes the ruler for whom the people rejoice, verse 2.

Quotes Proverbs 3:11 and 12 and teaches that no discipline seems enjoyable at the time but afterward yields a harvest of righteousness and peace. It reads the rod and discipline of verses 15 and 17 as the Father's training of His children.

The Rabshakeh asks what basis there is for the confidence of Hezekiah's people. It is verse 25 in real life: a great power appeals to fear, and the king of Judah, who trusted in the LORD, 2 Kings 18:5, is the one who stands.
Jesus tells His disciples not to be afraid of those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul, but to fear the One who can destroy both. It carries verse 25 into the ordeal of discipleship.

Peter and the apostles tell the council that they must obey God rather than men. It shows the proverb working in practice: when a human authority stands against the word of God, the one who trusts the LORD is set securely on high.

Isaac begins to tremble violently when he realises he has blessed Jacob and cannot take it back. The same family of Hebrew words as the 'fear' of verse 25 appears, which shows that the proverb has trembling in view.

study.oneStory:
Proverbs 29 sits at the end of a collection that began with kings, and it closes the kingly sayings by returning to the king's task and the people's condition. In the story of the Bible this is the long question that began after Eden: who will rule well? Adam was given dominion and failed. Israel asked for a king like the nations, 1 Samuel 8:5, and the kings who followed were, on the whole, like the nations. Hezekiah, who is praised for trusting the LORD, 2 Kings 18:5, still stumbled. The book of Proverbs holds out the ideal and the whole of the Old Testament waits for the one who can fulfil it.

The chapter also stands in the story of the word. Without revelation, the people run wild, as they did at Sinai with the golden calf. The Old Testament history is a long sequence of famines and abundances of the word, from the scarce visions of Samuel's youth to the prophets to the silence before the New Testament. Then the Word became flesh, and the Spirit came, so that God's people carry the word in their hearts.

The fear of man is the old snare, and its first trap was set in Eden, where the serpent said that God was withholding and the man and woman hid when they heard Him. Every later fear, of Pharaoh, of Assyria and of the council, comes after that first fear. Jesus is the new Adam who is not afraid, and who frees those who were slaves to fear.

The new creation takes the proverb to its end. There the king judges with perfect fairness, and the throne of God and of the Lamb is in the city, Revelation 22:3. The poor and the oppressor are not both there as they were, because the oppression is over, and the word is not scarce, because God Himself dwells with His people, Revelation 21:3. Nothing remains to be afraid of, and the righteous see His face, Revelation 22:4.

quiz.q: What happens to a man who remains stiff-necked after much reproof, verse 1?

options.text: He will suddenly be shattered beyond recovery.
options.note: Persistent refusal to heed correction leads to sudden, irreversible ruin.

options.text: He will eventually change his ways naturally.
options.note: This is the opposite of the verse's warning.

options.text: He will receive a final, gentle warning before consequences.
options.note: The verse describes sudden ruin, not another gentle warning.

options.text: He will face only minor, temporary setbacks.
options.note: The verse's language, 'shattered beyond recovery,' is far more severe than minor setbacks.

quiz.q: According to verse 2, what happens when the wicked rule?

options.text: The people groan.
options.note: Wicked leadership brings widespread suffering to those under it.

options.text: The people rejoice.
options.note: That is the effect of righteous flourishing, the opposite of wicked rule.

options.text: The people remain entirely unaffected.
options.note: The verse specifically ties leadership quality to the people's condition.

options.text: The people prosper economically despite moral decline.
options.note: The verse's plain claim is that the people groan, not that they prosper despite the wickedness.

quiz.q: What does verse 18 say happens where there is no vision (prophetic revelation)?

options.text: The people cast off restraint.
options.note: Without God's revealed word, a community loses its moral order.

options.text: The people automatically become more disciplined.
options.note: This is the opposite of the verse's warning.

options.text: Nothing changes for the community.
options.note: The verse specifically ties the absence of vision to disorder.

options.text: The people simply set their own alternate goals successfully.
options.note: The verse's concern, confirmed by its second half about keeping the Law, is the loss of restraint from lacking God's word, not merely needing alternate goals.

quiz.q: What does verse 17 promise about disciplining a son?

options.text: He will give you rest and bring delight to your soul.
options.note: Faithful discipline is tied to eventual peace and joy for the parent.

options.text: He will resent you permanently.
options.note: This is the opposite of the promised outcome.

options.text: It will make no difference to the parent's experience.
options.note: The verse specifically promises rest and delight as results of discipline.

options.text: It guarantees immediate, effortless obedience.
options.note: The verse promises eventual rest and delight, not necessarily immediate, effortless obedience.

options.text: The fear of man is a snare, but whoever trusts in the LORD is set securely on high.
options.note: Fearing people entraps, while trusting God secures true safety.

options.text: Fearing man and trusting the LORD produce identical results.
options.note: This is the opposite of the sharp contrast the verse draws.

options.text: Fearing man is safe as long as the person feared is powerful.
options.note: The verse calls the fear of man a snare regardless of who is feared.

options.text: Trusting the LORD is helpful but does not guarantee real security.
options.note: The verse's language, 'set securely on high,' is a strong and direct promise of safety, not a mere partial benefit.

questions: Verse 1 warns of sudden, irreversible ruin for those who remain stiff-necked after repeated correction. What correction have you been resisting that you need to finally receive?
Verse 2 ties a whole community's wellbeing to the character of its leaders. How does this shape the way you pray for, or think about, those in authority over you?
Verse 17 promises that disciplining a child brings the parent rest and delight. If you are raising children, what would more consistent, loving discipline look like this week?
Verse 18 warns that a people without God's revealed word casts off restraint. Where in your own life have you drifted because you have not been feeding regularly on Scripture?
Verse 25 calls the fear of man a snare. Whose opinion of you are you currently more afraid of than you are trusting in the LORD?

translationNotes.note: 'Stiff-necked' is a common Hebrew idiom for stubbornness, drawn from an ox resisting the pull of a yoke, used throughout the Old Testament, notably of Israel itself, Exodus 32:9.

'Vision' translates chazon, elsewhere always denoting prophetic revelation, not human ambition or planning; the KJV's famous rendering, 'where there is no vision, the people perish,' has often been popularly detached from this specific sense.
'A servant pampered from his youth' describes indulgent treatment producing later grief, an image paralleling the warnings elsewhere in Proverbs against failing to discipline a child, verse 15.
